title: The Black Diaspora and London
notes: Second edition. Every claim and relationship cites at least one consulted source. Places carry coordinates only where an official record supplies a grid reference (coordinate_status official_grid_reference); all others have null latitude and longitude.

people.summary: William Edward Burghardt Du Bois (1868–1963) was an African American sociologist, historian, and Pan-African organiser.
Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela (1918–2013) was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary, African National Congress leader, and first democratically elected President of South Africa (1994–1999).

Henry Sylvester Williams (born 1867 or 1869 – died on 26 March 1911 in Port of Spain) was a barrister, writer and local councillor in London; he published the journal *The Pan-African* (1901) and *The British Negro: A Factor in the Empire* (1902).
Amy Ashwood Garvey (1897 – 3 May 1969) was a Jamaican Pan-Africanist and feminist whose London clubs and networks served the anti-colonial movements of the 1930s and 1940s.
George Padmore (born Malcolm Ivan Meredith Nurse; 1902 or 1903 – died 23 September 1959) was a Trinidadian journalist and Pan-African organiser.
Olaudah Equiano (c.
Ignatius Sancho (c.
Mary Prince (born c.

William Cuffay (1788 – 1870) was a Black British tailor who became a leading London Chartist in the 1840s: Westminster's representative on the National Charter Association's metropolitan district council from 1841 and its treasurer from 1842.

Samuel Coleridge-Taylor (15 August 1875 – 1 September 1912) was a London-born composer and conductor of Sierra Leonean and English parentage who achieved international acclaim for *Hiawatha's Wedding Feast*.
Ladipo Solanke (c.

Harold Arundel Moody (1882 – 24 April 1947) was a Jamaican physician who practised medicine in Peckham, south London, from 1913 (from 1922 at 164 Queen's Road), and who founded the League of Coloured Peoples (LCP) in 1931; Fryer dates its founding meeting to 13 March 1931.

Una Maud Victoria Marson (1905–1965) was a Jamaican feminist poet, journalist and playwright who, during her second stay in England, worked as a broadcaster for the BBC World Service and started *Caribbean Voices*.
Cyril Lionel Robert James (1901 – 30 May 1989) was a Trinidadian historian and Marxist theorist; he died in London.

Constance Agatha Cummings-John (1918 – 21 February 2000) was a Sierra Leonean educator, politician and pioneer of African women's rights who trained as a teacher in London and was involved there in the West African Students' Union, the League of Coloured Peoples and the International African Service Bureau.

Kwame Nkrumah (21 September 1909 – 27 April 1972) was a Gold Coast revolutionary, Pan-African theorist, and Prime Minister of the Gold Coast from 1952 and the first Prime Minister of independent Ghana from 1957, then its President from 1960 until a military coup deposed him in 1966.
Jomo Kenyatta (c.

Claudia Jones (21 February 1915 – 24 December 1964) was a Trinidadian-born Communist theorist, Black feminist, and journalist who spent the final nine years of her life in political exile in London (1955–1964).

Paul Leroy Robeson (9 April 1898 – 23 January 1976) was an African American bass-baritone, actor, and anti-imperialist activist who made his home in London in the late 1920s and 1930s, returned to live in Britain in 1958, and began a long semi-retirement in the United States in 1963.

Oliver Reginald Kaizana Tambo (27 October 1917 – 23 April 1993) was a South African anti-apartheid leader who led the African National Congress from exile, as acting president after Chief Albert Luthuli's death and later as its President.

Beryl Agatha Gilroy (30 August 1924 – 4 April 2001) was a Guyanese novelist and educator who became Camden's first Black headteacher at Beckford Primary School in West Hampstead in 1969; the *Guardian* obituary calls her London's first Black head teacher.
Stuart McPhail Hall (3 February 1932 – 10 February 2014) was a Jamaican-born cultural theorist whose work reshaped modern understandings of race and diaspora identity.

Jessica Huntley (23 February 1927 – 13 October 2013) was a Guyanese activist and publisher who co-founded Bogle-L'Ouverture Publications in London in 1968; London Remembers gives her dates and dates the founding to 1969.
Altheia Jones-LeCointe (Althea Lecointe in Wild's thesis) is a Trinidadian who led the British Black Panther Movement in London.

Olive Elaine Morris was a Black feminist and community activist who squatted at 121 Railton Road in Brixton, was a founder member of the Brixton Black Women's Group (1973 or 1974) and worked to launch the Organisation of Women of African and Asian Descent (1978).

places.historical_address: Westminster (the building now known as Caxton Hall)
places.summary: The Victorian town hall in Caxton Street, Westminster, now known as Caxton Hall, where the First Pan-African Conference held its plenary sessions on 23–25 July 1900.
places.present_day: A Grade II listed building, 'No. 10, Caxton Hall', Caxton Street, SW1, on the National Heritage List for England (first listed 15 March 1984; entry amended 2018).
places.position_precision: 10-figure National Grid Reference given in the official list entry (to 1 metre); latitude and longitude converted from it

places.summary: The medieval hall of the Palace of Westminster, where Nelson Mandela, as President of South Africa, addressed both Houses of Parliament on 11 July 1996.
places.present_day: Part of the Houses of Parliament and the Palace of Westminster, listed at Grade I on the National Heritage List for England (first listed 5 February 1970).
places.position_precision: National Grid Reference given in the official list entry for the whole Palace of Westminster, not for Westminster Hall itself; latitude and longitude converted from it

places.summary: The South African embassy in Trafalgar Square, a focus of anti-apartheid protest, where Nelson Mandela later spoke.
The south London district at the centre of Black political organising from the late 1960s, visited by Nelson Mandela in 1996.
The Inn of Court in Holborn where Henry Sylvester Williams prepared for the Bar from 1897 and Kwame Nkrumah enrolled in 1945.
The college in central London where Henry Sylvester Williams studied from 1896 and, according to Fryer, Harold Moody studied medicine from 1904.
The house at 38 Church Street, Marylebone, which Westminster City Council describes as Henry Sylvester Williams's former home and marks with a green plaque.
places.present_day: Marked by a Westminster City Council green plaque to Henry Sylvester Williams, which the council describes as being at his former home.

places.summary: The Florence Mills Social Parlour, a nightclub and restaurant at 50 Carnaby Street, Soho, opened by Amy Ashwood Garvey in 1936; it became a gathering place for Black intellectuals and activists, including George Padmore and C. L. R. James.
Amy Ashwood Garvey's home at 1 Bassett Road, Ladbroke Grove, where a meeting on the 1958 riots was held and where a plaque to her was unveiled in 2009.
The flat at 22 Cranleigh Street (Cranleigh House), Somers Town, where George Padmore lived from 1941 to 1957 and where, according to Nkrumah, he and Padmore organised the 1945 Pan-African Congress.

The former town hall of Chorlton-on-Medlock, Manchester, where the Fifth Pan-African Congress met in October 1945; only its listed facade survives, in front of a Manchester Metropolitan University building.
places.present_day: The former town hall's facade is listed at Grade II and survives in front of a Manchester Metropolitan University building, which the university calls Grosvenor East and which carries a plaque commemorating the 1945 Congress.

places.summary: The parish church beside Westminster Abbey where Ignatius Sancho married Ann Osborne in 1758 and Olaudah Equiano was baptised in 1759.
No. 10 Union Street, near the Middlesex Hospital, the address from which Olaudah Equiano published and sold his Interesting Narrative in 1789.
Plasterers' Hall in Addle Street, City of London, where Olaudah Equiano was living when he made his will in May 1796.
The burial ground of Whitefield's Tabernacle in Tottenham Court Road, where Olaudah Equiano was buried on 6 April 1797.
The Duke of Montagu's residence in Whitehall, where Ignatius Sancho served the Montagu family as butler and valet.
The grocery shop at 19 Charles Street, Westminster, opened by Ignatius Sancho and his wife Ann in 1774, from which he wrote many of his letters.
Leigh Street, Bloomsbury, where Mary Prince lodged with her enslavers, the Woods, after arriving in London in 1828.
The office of the Anti-Slavery Society at 18 Aldermanbury, City of London, where Mary Prince sought help in November 1828.
Solly Terrace, Pentonville, where Thomas Pringle and his wife lived and where Mary Prince worked for them as a domestic servant from 1829.
The common-law court in which John Adams Wood's libel action against Thomas Pringle was heard on 27 February 1833, with Mary Prince as a witness.
The Orange Tree public house in Orange Street, Red Lion Square, Holborn, where the Chartist "Ulterior Committee" met in August 1848 and where police arrested eleven conspirators on 16 August.
The Central Criminal Court in the City of London, where William Cuffay was tried in 1848 and the Mangrove Nine in 1971.

places.historical_address: 15 Theobald's Road, Red Lion Square, Holborn
places.summary: The house at 15 Theobald's Road, Holborn, where the composer Samuel Coleridge-Taylor was born on 15 August 1875.

places.historical_address: The college's original building, later the home of the Royal College of Organists (Sayers)
places.summary: The original building of the Royal College of Music in Kensington, where Samuel Coleridge-Taylor studied from 1890.
University College London, in Bloomsbury, where Ladipo Solanke studied law, Kwame Nkrumah registered to read philosophy and Jomo Kenyatta worked as a language informant.

The first hostel of the West African Students' Union, known as Africa House, opened on Camden Road, London NW1, in 1933 with Ladipo Solanke as warden; WASU's journal gave its address as 62 Camden Road.
The West African Students' Union hostel at South Villas, Camden Square, bought freehold in 1938 and the subject of a long legal dispute.
Dr Harold Moody's home and surgery at 164 Queens Road, Peckham, from 1922 until his death in 1947, where Una Marson lodged from 1932 to 1935.
places.present_day: Marked by an English Heritage blue plaque, erected in 1995, inscribed 'DR HAROLD MOODY 1882-1947 Campaigner for Racial Equality lived and worked here'.

places.summary: The Central YMCA in Tottenham Court Road, London, where Harold Moody and his supporters founded the League of Coloured Peoples on 13 March 1931.
The Memorial Hall in Farringdon Street, London, a meeting hall used in the 1930s by the League of Coloured Peoples, the International African Friends of Abyssinia and other anti-colonial groups.
The house at 29 Brunswick Square, Camberwell, to which Una Marson moved from the Moodys' home in spring 1935.
The Scala Theatre in Charlotte Street, where Una Marson's play At What a Price ran for three nights from 15 January 1934.
The Abyssinian (Ethiopian) Legation at Princes Gate, Kensington, where Una Marson worked from October 1935 and for Emperor Haile Selassie during his exile.
The BBC's headquarters in Portland Place; Una Marson's biographer states that, although Marson worked for the BBC from 1941, she did not work in this building.
The top-floor flat at 9 Heathcote Street, Bloomsbury, formerly Nancy Cunard's, where C. L. R. James lived from 1934.
The Westminster Theatre, where the Stage Society staged C. L. R. James's play Toussaint Louverture, with Paul Robeson in the title role, on 15 and 16 March 1936.
Willesden, in north-west London, where C. L. R. James lived after returning to Britain in 1953.

The building at 165 Railton Road, Brixton, home from 1981 to 1989 of C. L. R. James, who lived in a flat above the offices of the journal Race Today; it carries an English Heritage blue plaque erected in 2004.
places.present_day: Marked by an English Heritage blue plaque, erected in 2004, inscribed 'C.L.R. JAMES 1901-1989 West Indian Writer and Political Activist lived and died here'.

places.summary: Whitelands College in Putney, the teacher-training college where Constance Cummings-John trained in the mid-1930s.
The University of London Institute of Education, which Beryl Gilroy joined in 1982 to work on multicultural education.

places.historical_address: 60 Burghley Road (Kentish Town, according to English Heritage; Tufnell Park, according to Sherwood)
places.summary: The house at 60 Burghley Road, north London, where Kwame Nkrumah rented a room from June 1945 to November 1947; it carries an English Heritage blue plaque erected in 2005.
places.present_day: Marked by an English Heritage blue plaque, erected in 2005, inscribed 'KWAME NKRUMAH 1909-1972 First President of Ghana lived here 1945-1947'.

places.summary: The London School of Economics, where Jomo Kenyatta studied social anthropology under Bronisław Malinowski from 1935 and Kwame Nkrumah attended lectures in 1945.
The small office at 94 Gray's Inn Road, Holborn, that served as the headquarters of the West African National Secretariat from late 1945, with Kwame Nkrumah as its general secretary.
The lodging house at 95 Cambridge Street, Pimlico, where Jomo Kenyatta stayed briefly in 1930 and lived from 1933 to 1937; it carries an English Heritage blue plaque erected in 2005.
places.present_day: Marked by an English Heritage blue plaque, erected in 2005, inscribed 'JOMO KENYATTA c1894-1978 First President of the Republic of Kenya lived here 1933-1937'.

places.summary: The rooms above Theo Campbell's record shop at 250 Brixton Road, where Claudia Jones edited the West Indian Gazette for most of its life, from 1958 until it moved to premises off Coldharbour Lane.
St Pancras Town Hall on Euston Road, venue of Claudia Jones's first Caribbean Carnival in 1959, of a Paul Robeson reception and of her memorial meeting in 1965.
Highgate Cemetery in north London, where the ashes of Claudia Jones were interred on 27 February 1965, next to the grave of Karl Marx.
The Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, where Paul Robeson sang in the London production of Show Boat in 1928 and gave a celebrated matinee concert on 3 July 1928.
The Savoy Theatre in the Strand, where Paul Robeson played Othello in 1930.
The Chestnuts, 1 Branch Hill, Hampstead, home of Paul Robeson in 1929–30; it carries an English Heritage blue plaque erected in 2002.
places.present_day: Marked by an English Heritage blue plaque, erected in 2002, inscribed 'PAUL ROBESON 1898-1976 Singer and Actor lived here 1929-1930'.

places.summary: The former London Institution building in Finsbury Circus, home of the School of Oriental Studies when Paul Robeson enrolled there in 1934.
The Royal Albert Hall in Kensington, where Paul Robeson gave a sold-out concert soon after his passport was restored in 1958.
The house in Muswell Hill, north London, bought by Adelaide Tambo, which was the family home of Oliver Tambo during his years of exile.
The building at 28 Penton Street, Islington, headquarters of the exiled African National Congress in Britain until 1994; South African agents bombed it on 14 March 1982.
Beckford Primary School in West Hampstead, where Beryl Gilroy became deputy head and then head teacher from 1968–9.
The Partisan coffee house at 7 Carlisle Street, Soho, which shared premises with the offices of Universities and Left Review, the journal Stuart Hall co-founded.
The secondary modern school in Stockwell, south London, where Stuart Hall worked as a supply teacher after moving to London.
The west London district of Notting Hill, scene of the 1958 riots, the founding of the British Black Panther Movement in 1968 and the Mangrove campaign.
Kilburn, in north-west London, where Stuart Hall and Catherine Hall bought a house together.
Rivington Place in Shoreditch, the arts building commissioned by Iniva and Autograph ABP, which opened in 2007 with Stuart Hall as the central figure in its creation.
The Huntleys' house at 141 Coldershaw Road, West Ealing, from which Bogle-L'Ouverture Publications worked from 1972 to 1975.
The Walter Rodney Bookshop at 5a Chignell Place, West Ealing, opened by Bogle-L'Ouverture in 1975 and repeatedly attacked by racists between 1977 and 1983.
Islington Town Hall, venue of the first International Book Fair of Radical Black and Third World Books in April 1982.

places.historical_name: Black Panther Movement premises, Shakespeare Road
places.historical_address: 38 Shakespeare Road, Brixton (base of the movement’s youth collective, according to Liz Obi)
places.summary: Shakespeare Road, Brixton, where the British Black Panther Movement had its centre from 1969, with a Black People's Information Centre at No. 38.

The Mangrove, Frank Crichlow's Caribbean restaurant at 8 All Saints Road, Notting Hill, opened in 1968; repeated police raids on it led to the march of 9 August 1970 and the trial of the Mangrove Nine.
The flat above a launderette at 121 Railton Road, Brixton, squatted by Olive Morris and Liz Obi from 1972–3; it later housed Sabarr Bookshop.
St Thomas' Hospital, Lambeth, where Olive Morris died on 12 July 1979.

events.name: First Pan-African Conference
events.summary: Three-day conference at Westminster Town Hall, 23–25 July 1900, convened by Henry Sylvester Williams's African Association; it founded the Pan-African Association and adopted the "Address to the Nations of the World".

events.name: First Universal Races Congress
events.summary: International congress on relations between "so-called white and so-called coloured peoples", held at the University of London on 26–29 July 1911; W. E. B. Du Bois was a United States secretary and gave a paper on the Negro race in America.

events.name: Second Pan-African Congress (London Session)
events.summary: The London sessions of the Second Pan-African Congress, held at Central Hall, Westminster, in late August 1921, before sessions in Brussels and Paris; convened by W. E. B. Du Bois, they adopted the outspoken "London Manifesto".

events.name: Fifth Pan-African Congress (Manchester)
events.summary: The Pan-African Congress held at Chorlton Town Hall, Manchester, in October 1945, organised by the Pan-African Federation, with W. E. B. Du Bois as International President; its declarations demanded colonial independence.

events.name: Nelson Mandela's Clandestine Visit
events.summary: Nelson Mandela's secret ten-day stay in London in June 1962, during his tour of Africa to win support for the ANC's armed struggle, when he saw Oliver Tambo and met British politicians.

events.name: Address in Westminster Hall
events.summary: Nelson Mandela's address as President of South Africa to both Houses of Parliament assembled in Westminster Hall on 11 July 1996.

events.name: Visit to Brixton
events.summary: Nelson Mandela's visit to Brixton, south London, in 1996, remembered by residents and recalled in the Commons tributes of 2013.

events.name: Baptism of Gustavus Vassa
events.summary: The baptism of the boy then called Gustavus Vassa, later known as Olaudah Equiano, at St Margaret's Church, Westminster, on 9 February 1759, with Miss Guerin as godmother.

events.name: Westminster Parliamentary Elections
events.summary: The Westminster parliamentary elections of 1774 and 1780, in which the grocer and writer Ignatius Sancho voted as a male householder.

events.name: Court of Common Pleas Trial (Pringle v. Cadell)
events.summary: Thomas Pringle's libel action against the London publisher Thomas Cadell, heard in the Court of Common Pleas on 21 February 1833, at which Mary Prince briefly gave evidence.

events.name: Court of King's Bench Trial (Wood v. Pringle)
events.summary: John Adams Wood's libel action against Thomas Pringle, heard in the Court of King's Bench on 27 February 1833, at which Mary Prince was the first defence witness and gave a detailed account of her life.

events.name: National Chartist Convention & Kennington Demo
events.summary: The National Chartist Convention, which assembled in London on 4 April 1848, and the mass meeting on Kennington Common on 10 April, whose processions William Cuffay's Demonstration Committee organised.

events.name: Police Raid on Orange Tree Public House
events.summary: The police raid of 16 August 1848 on the "Ulterior Committee" of Chartists and Irish Confederates meeting at the Orange Tree public house near Holborn, which ended a planned rising; William Cuffay, its secretary, was arrested two days later.

events.name: Old Bailey trial of William Cuffay et al. (September 1848 session)
events.summary: The trial of William Cuffay, William Lacey and Thomas Fay at the Central Criminal Court in the September 1848 session, for feloniously compassing to levy war against the Queen; Cuffay was convicted and transported for life.

events.name: Premiere of Hiawatha's Wedding Feast
events.summary: The first performance of Samuel Coleridge-Taylor's cantata Hiawatha's Wedding Feast, at a Royal College of Music concert conducted by Sir Charles Stanford on 11 November 1898.

events.name: Founding of WASU
events.summary: The meeting of West African students in London in August 1925 at which, after a heated debate, the West African Students' Union was founded, with J. B. Danquah as president and Ladipo Solanke as secretary-general.

events.name: Founding Meeting of LCP
events.summary: The meeting at the Central YMCA, Tottenham Court Road, on 13 March 1931 at which Dr Harold Moody and his supporters founded the League of Coloured Peoples.

events.name: Staging of Toussaint Louverture
events.summary: The Stage Society's production of C. L. R. James's play Toussaint Louverture at the Westminster Theatre in March 1936, with Paul Robeson in the title role.

events.name: Caribbean Carnival
events.summary: The first Caribbean Carnival organised by the West Indian Gazette, held indoors at St Pancras Town Hall on Friday 30 January 1959 and partly televised by the BBC, in response to the 1958 riots.

events.name: Othello at the Savoy Theatre (opening night)
events.summary: The opening night, 19 May 1930, of Maurice Browne's production of Othello at the Savoy Theatre, London, with Paul Robeson as Othello and Peggy Ashcroft as Desdemona.

events.name: ANC Office Bombing
events.summary: The bombing of the African National Congress's London headquarters at 28 Penton Street, Islington, on the morning of Sunday 14 March 1982, by agents of the South African security services.

events.name: International Book Fair of Radical Black and Third World Books (first fair)
events.summary: The first International Book Fair of Radical Black and Third World Books, a week-long festival at Islington Town Hall in April 1982, planned by John La Rose, Jessica and Eric Huntley and others from January 1981.

events.name: Black People's Day of Action
events.summary: The Black People's Day of Action of Monday 2 March 1981, a national march through London called by the New Cross Massacre Action Committee to protest at the official and press response to the New Cross fire.

events.name: Mangrove Demo
events.summary: The march of Sunday 9 August 1970 from the Mangrove restaurant in All Saints Road, Notting Hill, to protest at repeated police raids on the restaurant, organised by the Action Committee for Defence of the Mangrove with the Black Panther Movement.

events.name: Mangrove Nine Trial
events.summary: The trial of the Mangrove Nine at the Old Bailey, from 5 October to mid-December 1971, at which all nine were acquitted of incitement to riot and the judge acknowledged "evidence of racial hatred on both sides".

events.name: Clement Gomwalk Incident
events.summary: The arrest of the Nigerian diplomat Clement Gomwalk by police in Brixton on 15 November 1969, in which the seventeen-year-old Olive Morris intervened and was arrested and, by her own account, beaten.

organisations.name: African Association
organisations.summary: Black-led association founded in London in 1897 or 1898 by Henry Sylvester Williams to lobby for Africans and people of African descent in the British Empire; it called the 1900 Pan-African Conference and merged into the Pan-African Association.

organisations.name: African National Congress
organisations.summary: The South African liberation movement founded in 1912, banned in South Africa from 1960 to 1990; its external mission under Oliver Tambo made London one of its bases, with a headquarters at 28 Penton Street, Islington, that South African agents bombed in 1982.

organisations.name: Honourable Society of Gray's Inn
organisations.summary: One of the Inns of Court in Holborn, where Henry Sylvester Williams prepared for the Bar from 1897 and Kwame Nkrumah enrolled in 1945.

organisations.name: King's College London
organisations.summary: The London college where Henry Sylvester Williams studied from 1896 and where, according to Fryer, Harold Moody studied medicine from 1904.

organisations.name: St Marylebone Borough Council
organisations.summary: The London borough council to which Henry Sylvester Williams was elected in November 1906 as a Progressive for the Church Street ward.

organisations.name: Nigerian Progress Union
organisations.summary: Union of Nigerian students in London founded in July 1924 by Ladipo Solanke and others with Amy Ashwood Garvey's encouragement, to promote Nigerian welfare and mass education; a forerunner of the West African Students' Union.

organisations.name: International African Friends of Abyssinia
organisations.summary: The International African Friends of Abyssinia, formed in London in 1935 by C. L. R. James, Amy Ashwood Garvey and others to oppose Italy's threatened invasion of Ethiopia; it held rallies at the Memorial Hall and Trafalgar Square and disbanded in 1936.

organisations.name: International African Service Bureau
organisations.summary: The International African Service Bureau, launched in London in 1937 by George Padmore, C. L. R. James, I. T. A. Wallace-Johnson, Ras Makonnen and others to inform British opinion about the colonies and press for African self-determination; it joined the Pan-African Federation in 1944.

organisations.name: Sons of Africa
organisations.summary: The name under which a group of Black abolitionists in London, among them Olaudah Equiano and Ottobah Cugoano, signed letters and addresses against the slave trade in the later 1780s.

organisations.name: Anti-Slavery Society
organisations.summary: The London society founded in 1823 to campaign for the abolition of colonial slavery, known as the Anti-Slavery Society; Thomas Pringle was its secretary from 1827, and Mary Prince sought its help at its office at 18 Aldermanbury in 1828.

organisations.name: National Charter Association
organisations.summary: The membership organisation of the Chartist movement, founded at Manchester in July 1840 and wound up in 1860; William Cuffay represented Westminster on its London district council from 1841 and was the council's treasurer from 1842.

organisations.name: Royal College of Music
organisations.summary: The London conservatoire where Samuel Coleridge-Taylor studied from 1890 to 1897, and where Hiawatha's Wedding Feast was first performed in 1898.

organisations.name: University College London (UCL)
organisations.summary: The London college where Ladipo Solanke studied law from 1923 to 1927, where Kwame Nkrumah registered to read philosophy, and where Jomo Kenyatta worked as a language informant.

organisations.name: West African Students' Union (WASU)
organisations.summary: The West African Students' Union, founded in London in August 1925 with Ladipo Solanke as secretary-general; it ran the Africa House hostel, published the journal Wasu, lobbied the Colonial Office and became a training ground for West African nationalist leaders.

organisations.name: League of Coloured Peoples (LCP)
organisations.summary: The League of Coloured Peoples, founded in London on 13 March 1931 by Dr Harold Moody, who led it until his death in 1947; a welfare and pressure group that published The Keys, campaigned against the colour bar and drafted a "Charter for Coloured Peoples" in 1944.

organisations.name: British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC)
organisations.summary: The national broadcaster for which Una Marson worked during the Second World War, as a programme assistant on the Empire Service from 1941 and as the founder of Caribbean Voices.

organisations.name: Whitelands College
organisations.summary: The teacher-training college in Putney where Constance Cummings-John trained as a teacher in the mid-1930s.

organisations.name: London School of Economics (LSE)
organisations.summary: The London college where Jomo Kenyatta studied social anthropology under Bronisław Malinowski from 1935, and where Kwame Nkrumah attended lectures in 1945.

organisations.name: West African National Secretariat (WANS)
organisations.summary: The West African National Secretariat, formed in London in late 1945 after the Manchester Congress, with Kwame Nkrumah as general secretary, to work for "a free, united, independent and democratic West Africa"; it collapsed soon after Nkrumah left for the Gold Coast in 1947.

organisations.name: Committee of Afro-Asian Caribbean Organisations (CAACO)
organisations.summary: The Committee of Afro-Asian Caribbean Organisations, a London coalition initiated by Claudia Jones and the West Indian Gazette in the early 1960s, which campaigned against racial discrimination and the Commonwealth Immigrants Act and in solidarity with the US civil rights movement.

organisations.name: School of Oriental Studies (SOAS)
organisations.summary: The London school where Paul Robeson enrolled to study Swahili and phonetics in 1934, and where Jomo Kenyatta worked as a language informant.

organisations.name: Iniva & Autograph ABP
organisations.summary: The Institute of International Visual Arts and Autograph ABP (the Association of Black Photographers), the two arts organisations, both chaired by Stuart Hall, that commissioned Rivington Place in Shoreditch.

organisations.name: Bogle-L'Ouverture Publications
organisations.summary: The Ealing-based Black publishing house founded by Jessica and Eric Huntley in 1968 or 1969, named after Paul Bogle and Toussaint L'Ouverture; it first published Walter Rodney's The Groundings with My Brothers, ran the Walter Rodney Bookshop and co-founded the International Book Fair of Radical Black and Third World Books.

organisations.name: British Black Panther Movement
organisations.summary: The British Black Panther Movement, founded in Notting Hill in 1968 by Obi Egbuna and led from the end of that year by Altheia Jones-LeCointe from Brixton; it took part in the Mangrove campaign and in 1973 renamed itself the Black Workers Movement.

organisations.name: Brixton Black Women's Group
organisations.summary: An autonomous Black women's group formed in Brixton in 1973 or 1974, largely by women from the Black Power organisations; Olive Morris was a founder member, and the group published Speak Out, helped set up OWAAD and initiated the Brixton Defence Campaign after 1981.

organisations.name: Organisation of Women of African and Asian Descent
organisations.summary: The Organisation of Women of African and Asian Descent (OWAAD), a national network of Black women's groups formed in February 1978 after a meeting at Warwick University; it held national conferences from 1979, published FOWAAD, and broke up in 1982 or 1983.

works.title: To the Nations of the World
works.summary: The address adopted by the First Pan-African Conference in London in July 1900, signed by Alexander Walters, Henry B. Brown, Henry Sylvester Williams and W. E. B. Du Bois; it contains the first version of Du Bois's phrase on "the problem of the color line".

works.title: Address in Westminster Hall
works.summary: Nelson Mandela's address to both Houses of Parliament in Westminster Hall on 11 July 1996.

works.title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano
works.summary: Olaudah Equiano's autobiography, published by subscription in London in 1789 from his lodging in Union Street; a founding work of Black British writing and an abolitionist text.

works.title: Letters of the Late Ignatius Sancho, an African
works.summary: The collected letters of Ignatius Sancho, published in two volumes in London in 1782, two years after his death, with a memoir of his life; they were reissued in a third edition in 1784.

works.title: Minuets, Cotillons & Country Dances
works.summary: Ignatius Sancho's first published collection of dance music, 'Composed by an African' and dedicated to the Duke of Buccleuch, published in London in the 1760s.

works.title: The History of Mary Prince, a West Indian Slave
works.summary: Mary Prince's account of her life in slavery in Bermuda, Turks Island and Antigua and of her escape in London, dictated to Susanna Strickland and published by Thomas Pringle in 1831; the first narrative of a Black British woman's escape from slavery.

works.title: Hiawatha's Wedding Feast
works.summary: Samuel Coleridge-Taylor's cantata setting part of Longfellow's The Song of Hiawatha, first performed at the Royal College of Music on 11 November 1898; it made him famous and became the first part of his Hiawatha trilogy.

works.title: Twenty-Four Negro Melodies, Op. 59
works.summary: Samuel Coleridge-Taylor's Twenty-Four Negro Melodies, transcribed for the piano, Op. 59, published in Boston in 1905 with a preface by Booker T. Washington.

works.title: Wasu (Journal)
works.summary: The journal of the West African Students' Union, launched in London in March 1926; its Yoruba title means "Preach", and it carried political and cultural writing by West Africans, including Ladipo Solanke.

works.title: The Keys
works.summary: The quarterly journal of the League of Coloured Peoples, published from 1933, which printed the League's aims in every issue; Una Marson edited it in its early years.

works.title: At What a Price
works.summary: Una Marson's first play, a comedy first staged in Kingston in June 1932 and then by the League of Coloured Peoples in London in November 1933 and at the Scala Theatre in January 1934.

works.title: Caribbean Voices
works.summary: The BBC radio programme for Caribbean writing devised by Una Marson, first broadcast on 11 March 1943 and running until 1958.

works.title: International African Opinion
works.summary: The journal of the International African Service Bureau, first issued in July 1938 with C. L. R. James as its editor; it circulated among colonial Africans and argued for anti-colonial struggle based on "the great masses of the people".

works.title: Toussaint Louverture (Play)
works.summary: C. L. R. James's play about the leader of the Haitian Revolution, written in 1934 and staged by the Stage Society at the Westminster Theatre on 15 and 16 March 1936 with Paul Robeson in the title role.

works.title: The Black Jacobins
works.summary: C. L. R. James's history of the Haitian Revolution, The Black Jacobins: Toussaint Louverture and the San Domingo Revolution, published in London by Secker and Warburg in September 1938.

works.title: A History of Negro Revolt
works.summary: C. L. R. James's short survey of Black resistance and revolt, written for Raymond Postgate's Fact series and published in September 1938.

works.title: The New African
works.summary: The monthly paper of the West African National Secretariat, edited in London by Kwame Nkrumah, which first appeared in March 1946.

works.title: Towards Colonial Freedom
works.summary: Kwame Nkrumah's pamphlet against colonial rule, drafted in the United States and published in London in 1947.

works.title: Facing Mount Kenya
works.summary: Jomo Kenyatta's study of Kikuyu life, based on his London School of Economics diploma thesis and published by Secker and Warburg in September 1938 with an introduction by Bronisław Malinowski.

works.title: Sanders of the River
works.summary: Alexander Korda's 1935 film of Edgar Wallace's colonial adventure stories, starring Paul Robeson as Bosambo, in which Jomo Kenyatta appeared as an extra.

works.title: West Indian Gazette
works.summary: The monthly newspaper founded and edited by Claudia Jones in London in 1958, later titled West Indian Gazette and Afro-Asian-Caribbean News; it campaigned against racism, sponsored the first Caribbean Carnival and closed after her death.

works.title: Black Teacher
works.summary: Beryl Gilroy's memoir of her years as a teacher in London, first published in 1976.

works.title: Frangipani House
works.summary: Beryl Gilroy's first novel, set in an old people's home in Guyana, published by Heinemann in 1986.

works.title: New Left Review
works.summary: The journal of the British New Left, formed in January 1960 from Universities and Left Review and The New Reasoner, with Stuart Hall as its first editor.

works.title: The Groundings with My Brothers
works.summary: Walter Rodney's talks on Black Power and African history given in Jamaica in 1968, published in London in 1969 as the first book of Bogle-L'Ouverture Publications.

claims.claim_text: Born in 1868 and died in 1963.
Attended the 1900 First Pan-African Conference.
Chaired the committee for 'To the Nations of the World'.
Hon. Secretary for the United States of the First Universal Races Congress (London, July 1911), to which he contributed the paper 'The Negro Race in the United States of America'.
Took the initiative to hold the 1921 Second Pan-African Congress, held in Paris, London and Brussels.
Holt says that Du Bois co-chaired the opening session; Padmore's proceedings put him alone in the chair on 16 October.
Born 18 July 1918; died 5 December 2013.
Visited London in June 1962.
Spoke at Westminster Hall on 11 July 1996.
Delivered official address to Parliament.
Visited Brixton in 1996.
Spoke at South Africa House (Hansard recollection).
Birth disputed: earlier biographers gave 19 February 1869 in Arouca, Trinidad; Sherwood reports a Barbados birth registration dated 24 March 1867.
His family moved to Arouca, Trinidad, shortly after his birth, and he always identified himself as Trinidadian.
His family moved from Barbados, where he was born, to Arouca in Trinidad shortly after his birth.
Studied at King's College, London, from 1896: Afropean says law; Adi & Sherwood say he enrolled as an evening student taking Latin.
Admitted to Gray's Inn in 1897 (Adi & Sherwood); qualified and practised there (Afropean); called to the Bar in June 1902.
Organised the 1900 Pan-African Conference.
Attended 1900 Conference alongside Du Bois.
Elected to Marylebone Council in 1906.
Commemorated at 38 Church Street.
Origin Jamaica.
Helped organise Nigerian Progress Union.
Operated Florence Mills Social Parlour.
Member of IAFA.
Co-founded IASB.
Commemorated by plaque at 1 Bassett Road; unveiled 5 November 2009.
Padmore records that she chaired the opening session of 15 October; Holt says that she co-chaired it with Du Bois.
Counted by Claudia Jones among her friends (English Heritage).
Birth year disputed (1903 vs 1902).
Origin Trinidad.
Became Kwame Nkrumah's adviser on African affairs after Ghana's independence in 1957.
Settled in London in 1935.
Co-founded IASB.
Resided at 22 Cranleigh Street.
Hosted meetings at 22 Cranleigh Street.
Participated in 1945 Congress.
Holt records Du Bois joining Amy Jacques Garvey and George Padmore in sponsoring the 1945 Congress.
Collaborated with C. L. R. James and Amy Ashwood Garvey to form the IASB.
Birthplace disputed between Essaka, Igboland (autobiography) and South Carolina (naval and baptismal records).
Baptised at St Margaret's, Westminster, on 9 February 1759.
Title page of the 1789 first edition gives the author's address as No. 10, Union-Street, Middlesex Hospital.
One of the leaders of the Black abolitionists in London who styled themselves the Sons of Africa; led several of their delegations to the Houses of Parliament.
Authored and self-published The Interesting Narrative in 1789.
Drew up his will on 28 May 1796 while living in Plasterers' Hall, Addle Street, in the City of London.
Served the Duchess of Montagu as butler until her death, then the Duke as his valet, until gout ended his service towards the close of 1773.
Kept a grocer's shop with his wife after leaving the Duke's service towards the close of 1773.
Voted in the 1774 and 1780 Westminster parliamentary elections.
Married Ann Osborne at St Margaret's, Westminster, on 17 December 1758.
Authored letters published posthumously in 1782.
Brought to Leigh Street, Bloomsbury in 1828 by the Woods.
Took her trunk to the Moravian missionaries at Hatton Garden after the Woods turned her out.
Sought assistance from the Anti-Slavery Society.
Lived with the Pringles in Pentonville as their domestic servant from 1829; their lodger Susanna Strickland took down her life story.
Dictated her history to Susanna Strickland; it was published in London in 1831.
Briefly gave evidence in Pringle v. Cadell, heard in the Court of Common Pleas on 21 February 1833, to confirm that she had dictated her account for Pringle; she was not cross-examined.

Gave evidence, as the first defence witness, in Wood's libel action against Pringle, heard in the Court of King's Bench on 27 February 1833 and reported in The Times on 1 March 1833 (Lambert); Salih's notes date the case to March 1833.
Westminster's representative on the National Charter Association's metropolitan district council from 1841, and its treasurer from 1842.
Delegate to the April 1848 National Chartist Convention and chair of the 'Demonstration Committee' for the 10 April meeting on Kennington Common.
Arrested on the evening of 18 August 1848 at his lodging, 11 Hollins Street, Wardour Street, Soho, two days after the arrests at the Orange Tree (16 August).

Tried at the Central Criminal Court in the September 1848 session with William Lacey and Thomas Fay for feloniously compassing to levy war against the Queen; found guilty and sentenced to transportation for life.
Born at 15 Theobald's Road, Holborn, on 15 August 1875.
Studied at the Royal College of Music from the Christmas Term 1890 to the end of the Easter Term 1897.
Hiawatha's Wedding Feast was first performed at a Royal College of Music concert on 11 November 1898, conducted by Sir Charles Stanford.
Elected to the executive committee of the Pan-African Association, into which the African Association was merged at the July 1900 conference.
Participated in the 1900 First Pan-African Conference.
Du Bois first saw him at a gathering in London, met him several times at public gatherings and visited his home (year not stated).
In a letter of 3 January 1904 he called Du Bois's The Souls of Black Folk 'about the finest book I have ever read by a coloured man, and one of the best by any author, white or black'.
Died 27 August 1963.
Died in Jamaica 3 May 1969.
Died 23 September 1959.
George Padmore was born Malcolm Ivan Meredith Nurse.
Died at his home in Johannesburg on 5 December 2013.
Died on 26 March 1911 (Adi & Sherwood); in Port of Spain, aged 44 (Afropean).
Wrote for Wasu, the WASU journal launched in March 1926, and for a time had editorial responsibility for it.
First warden of Africa House, the WASU hostel opened on Camden Road in 1933.
Born 1882, died 1947.
Origin Jamaica.
Practice at 164 Queen's Road.
Founded the League of Coloured Peoples in 1931.
The LCP issued its quarterly journal The Keys by 1933.
Born 1905, died 1965.
Origin Jamaica.
Lodged with the Moody family at 164 Queen's Road, Peckham, from July 1932 until spring 1935.
Secretary of the League of Coloured Peoples in London (Busby); its unpaid assistant secretary from autumn 1933 (Jarrett-Macauley).
Edited the League of Coloured Peoples' journal, The Keys.
Directed her play At What a Price at the Scala Theatre, Charlotte Street, in a three-night run from 15 January 1934, after a League performance on 23 November 1933.
Worked for the Abyssinian (Ethiopian) Legation in Kensington from October 1935, through the Emperor's arrival in 1936.
Radio broadcaster with the BBC World Service during her second stay in England, from 1938.
Started the BBC programme Caribbean Voices.
Born 1901, died 1989.
Origin Trinidad.
Lived at 9 Heathcote Street, Bloomsbury, for several years from 1934.
Founded and led the International African Friends of Abyssinia in 1935.
His play Toussaint Louverture was staged in 1936, with Paul Robeson leading the cast.
Co-founded IASB.
Published The Black Jacobins.
Published A History of Negro Revolt.
After returning to London in 1953, lived for five years in Hampstead and Willesden (street not stated).
Resided at 165 Railton Road.
Born 1918, died 2000.
Origin Sierra Leone.
Trained as a teacher at Whitelands College in Putney, having gone to England at seventeen.
Involved in the League of Coloured Peoples, led by Harold Moody, while training as a teacher in London.
Became involved in the International African Service Bureau in London after study in the United States.
Birth date recorded by the priest who baptised him as 21 September 1909, the date he used on official documents; he himself thought 18 September 1909 likely.
Resided at 60 Burghley Road.
Enrolled at Gray's Inn and attended lectures at the LSE on arriving in London; later also registered at University College.
Worked with George Padmore organising the 1945 Manchester Pan-African Congress.
One of the founders and general secretary of the West African National Secretariat, formed after the 1945 Congress.
Lived at 95 Cambridge Street 1933–37, after a short stay there in 1930.
Worked at University College London as a linguistic informant, including for Lilias Armstrong's work on Kikuyu phonology.
Attended the London School of Economics, working for a diploma in anthropology under Bronisław Malinowski.
Attended Fifth Pan-African Congress.
Arrived in London.
Founded the West Indian Gazette in 1958.
Organised the indoor Caribbean Carnival.
Starred in Show Boat at Drury Lane in 1928.
Opened as Othello at the Savoy Theatre, London, on 19 May 1930.
Led the cast of C. L. R. James's play Toussaint Louverture in 1936.
Lived, when in London, at the house in Muswell Hill that his wife Adelaide bought after some fifteen years of hospital shift work.
Mandela visited him in London during his 1962 trip abroad.
When in London, held early-morning meetings at the ANC Mission, 28 Penton Street, its UK headquarters.
Became headteacher of Beckford Primary School in 1969.
Edited New Left Review in 1960–1961, after editing Universities & Left Review in 1957–1959.
Took part, through the New Left's ULR Club, in anti-racist work in Notting Hill after his arrival in London, including helping to put together local black and white tenants' defence associations.
Had a house in Kilburn, which he describes as 'the house we bought together'; Catherine Hall's mother later had her own flat there.
Jessica and Eric Huntley co-founded Bogle-L'Ouverture Publications in 1968 (British Library) or 1969 (London Remembers).
Operated the bookshop at 5a Chignell Place, West Ealing (renamed the Walter Rodney Bookshop in 1980)
Led the British Black Panther Movement.
Helped set up the action group behind the Mangrove demonstration of 9 August 1970, and was tried for riot at the march.

At the 1971 Mangrove Nine trial she was acquitted of the most serious charges (riot) but convicted of causing an affray and of assaulting police officers; sentenced to fifteen months' imprisonment, suspended for two years.
Intervened in the police arrest of the Nigerian diplomat Clement Gomwalk in Brixton on 15 November 1969, and was beaten by the police.
Squatted a flat at 121 Railton Road with Liz Turnbull (Liz Obi) from 1972 (libcom) or 1973 (Lambeth Archives catalogue), resisting attempts at eviction.
Birth year disputed: c. 1884 (Adi & Sherwood, 2003) or 1886 (Adi, 1998).
Origin Nigeria.
Studied law at University College London, 1923–7.
Founded the Nigerian Progress Union in 1924 with the assistance of Amy Ashwood Garvey.
Founded the West African Students' Union in 1925 with Herbert Bankole-Bright and became its first secretary-general.
Jessica Huntley's household and publishing activity moved to 141 Coldershaw Road in 1972.
Claudia Jones's newspaper, the West Indian Gazette, had offices at 250 Brixton Road.
Paul Robeson enrolled at SOAS to study Swahili and phonetics in 1934.
Lived at The Chestnuts, 1 Branch Hill, Hampstead, 1929–30
One of the founder members of the Brixton Black Women's Group, formed in 1973 (The Heart of the Race) or 1974 (Lambeth Archives catalogue; Liz Obi).
Conducted her own defence at the 1971 Mangrove Nine trial at the Old Bailey; all nine defendants were acquitted of the most serious charges.

Co-founded the Partisan Coffee House at 7 Carlisle Street, Soho, in 1958 with Raphael Samuel and Eric Hobsbawm (Bishopsgate); Hall's own account credits the café to Samuel. Universities and Left Review had offices upstairs, where Hall edited the journal.
Played Othello at the Savoy Theatre from 19 May 1930.
On 18 January 1981 attended the meeting at John La Rose's home in Finsbury Park called to discuss holding the Book Fair, first held in April 1982; later one of the fair's joint directors.
One of the 'Old Bailey Three', arrested with Darcus Howe and Abdul Macintosh after a scuffle with police outside the Old Bailey on 20 June 1971.
Claudia Jones and Paul Robeson were friends and political colleagues in New York and London; in 1959–60 her West Indian Gazette held receptions and a concert featuring Robeson.
George Padmore and Jomo Kenyatta worked together from 1930, in Padmore's Comintern-backed International Trade Union Committee of Negro Workers and later in London's IAFA and IASB.
C. L. R. James and Jomo Kenyatta worked together in the IAFA (James chairman, Kenyatta honorary secretary); James introduced Kenyatta to his publisher and reviewed Facing Mount Kenya.
C. L. R. James and Amy Ashwood Garvey, who had met through the League of Coloured Peoples, together revived the committee that became the IAFA in 1935, and both were officers of the IASB in 1937.
Amy Ashwood Garvey and Claudia Jones were friends and colleagues in London; Jones was general secretary of Ashwood Garvey's Association for the Advancement of Coloured People, founded in 1958.
Jomo Kenyatta, arriving in London in March 1929, went to Ladipo Solanke, whose West African Students' Union had promised the Kikuyu Central Association hospitality; Adi records their friendship.
Jomo Kenyatta and Paul Robeson met while making Sanders of the River (1934–35); Murray-Brown records that they became better acquainted and visited each other's flats.
Stuart Hall held a recorded conversation with C. L. R. James, published as 'A Conversation with C. L. R. James' (1996), and wrote 'C.L.R. James: A Portrait' (1992).
